messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mr. Nguyen is a 60-year-old South Eastern Asian male who has been working as a hotel manager for over three decades. His life took an unexpected turn when he was exposed to toxic chemicals during a renovation at the hotel where he worked. The incident occurred on a busy afternoon, and despite wearing protective gear, he inhaled the fumes when a ventilation system malfunctioned. Mr. Nguyen vividly remembers the metallic taste of the chemical lingering in his mouth as he gasped for air, an experience that has left indelible marks on his memory. Since then, Mr. Nguyen has found himself constantly checking his body for signs of danger or injury. He feels that his body is no longer reliable and can’t trust it to protect him from further harm. This sense of helplessness has only deepened as he struggles with the belief that he cannot prevent bad things from happening to him. As a result, he often avoids conversations where coworkers might remind him of the event, exacerbating his feelings of isolation and alienation. Mr. Nguyen’s experience of the event has left him feeling as though he belongs nowhere. This pervasive sense of helplessness drives him to constantly monitor his surroundings for any signs of threat. Even mundane delays can trigger a cascade of assumptions about impending danger. His body feels perpetually tense, ready to react to perceived threats that aren’t actually present. The memory of the toxic chemical exposure is so vivid that it forces its way into his mind unexpectedly, often when he least expects it. He can taste the metallic residue again and again as if the event were happening in real-time. This uncontrolled access to memories has led him to avoid certain places or situations where triggers might be present, reinforcing his belief that he cannot trust himself or his surroundings. When Mr. Nguyen does encounter these reminders, whether from a colleague’s casual comment or an unexpected delay, he reacts as if he is in immediate danger, even though nothing tangible is threatening him. This heightened state of alertness has led to increased tension and anxiety in his daily life, both at work and at home. His partner notices the changes but feels helpless to support him effectively. Mr. Nguyen’s avoidance behaviors have taken a toll on his relationships and professional environment. He frequently scans his surroundings for signs of potential threats, which can make it difficult to focus during meetings or when managing hotel operations. This constant vigilance has caused friction with coworkers who don’t understand why he reacts so intensely to minor issues. The vividness of the memory and its uncontrolled access often lead him to feel like he is reliving the event over and over again, reinforcing his belief that his body cannot be trusted. His heightened sense of threat and helplessness are perpetuated by these intrusive memories, creating a self-reinforcing cycle where each component feeds into the other. The weight of these experiences has become unbearable for Mr. Nguyen, leading him to seek professional help. He is most afraid of being unable to protect himself or his loved ones from further harm but also hopes that through therapy he can regain some sense of control and trust in himself and his surroundings. The realization that he needs assistance to break this cycle of fear and avoidance has finally motivated him to take the step towards healing.
